name: Fall of Tenochtitlan
info: A Spanish force under Hernán Cortés and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, above all Tlaxcalans, besieged the Mexica capital Tenochtitlan in 1521, starved it, and took it on 13 August, after which the city was sacked.

facts.date: May to 13 August 1521 (Julian date); the three Spanish forces took up their positions on 22 May and the Mexica surrendered on 13 August
facts.place: Tenochtitlan, the island capital of the Mexica in Lake Texcoco, and the causeways and lakeside towns round it, in the Valley of Mexico, present-day Mexico
facts.sides: The Spaniards under Hernán Cortés, with 84 horsemen, 194 crossbowmen and arquebusiers, 650 foot soldiers, thirteen sloops and 20,000 warriors from Tlaxcala, Huexotzinco and Cholula, besieged the Mexica under their tlatoani Cuauhtémoc; Cortés's own letter puts his allies at the end at more than 150,000 against some 900 Spaniards
facts.outcome: The Mexica surrendered on 13 August 1521 and Cuauhtémoc was captured. Estimates of the dead in the campaign run from 100,000 to 240,000, and the Indigenous allies went on killing and looting after the surrender.

t: Cortés took the city with the help of Indigenous allies, mainly Tlaxcalans, who had been subjugated by the Mexica; they were indispensable to his success.
A smallpox epidemic that began in October 1520 killed much of the Mexica leadership, among them the tlatoani Cuitlahuac, and weakened a city that the Spaniards then cut off from food and water.
After the surrender the Indigenous allies slaughtered thousands of civilians; Cortés wrote that he could not prevent more than fifteen thousand being killed and sacrificed in one day.
dyk: Cortés ordered thirteen sloops built in Tlaxcala and launched them on Lake Texcoco in 1521; with them he could open gaps in the causeways and control the water round Tenochtitlan.
ev: Cortés lands at San Juan de Ulúa with 508 soldiers, 100 sailors and 14 small cannons
The Spaniards enter Tenochtitlan and take Moctezuma hostage
On La Noche Triste the Spaniards flee Tenochtitlan along the Tlacopan causeway with heavy losses
Smallpox breaks out in Tenochtitlan and kills Cuitlahuac, who is followed by Cuauhtémoc
Cortés launches thirteen sloops on Lake Texcoco and begins the blockade
Three Spanish forces with their allies take up positions at Tacuba, Coyohuacan and Ixtlapalapan
The Mexica surrender and Cuauhtémoc is captured, after which the city is sacked
Cuauhtémoc is hanged for treason during a Spanish expedition to Guatemala

sections.background:
In April 1519 Hernán Cortés landed at San Juan de Ulúa with 508 soldiers, 100 sailors and 14 small cannons. Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar, the Governor of Cuba, had revoked his mandate before he sailed, so Cortés created a local government at Veracruz and had himself elected its magistrate, answerable in theory only to the King of Spain. He landed on the borders of Cempoala, a vassal state of the Aztecs with many grievances against them, and met other polities that resented Aztec rule. The Tlaxcalans gave him two battles in a day and one at night before they began to consider his offers of peace; Xicotencatl the Elder wanted an alliance against the Aztecs, which was also Cortés's aim.

In November 1519 the Spaniards entered Tenochtitlan and were received amicably by Moctezuma II. On 14 November they took him hostage as a safety measure, because they were so outnumbered. Why Moctezuma cooperated is uncertain. Cortés knew little of how the Aztecs were ruled, and as Moctezuma obeyed his orders his authority slipped.

Cortés left Pedro de Alvarado in the city with 80 soldiers and marched to the coast against the force Velázquez had sent under Pánfilo de Narváez, which he defeated and absorbed. At the festival of Toxcatl Alvarado ordered the gates of the patio closed and killed many thousands of Aztec nobles, warriors and priests. The massacre turned all the Aztecs against the Spanish and undermined Moctezuma's authority.
sections.forces:
For the siege Cortés had 84 horsemen, 194 crossbowmen and arquebusiers and 650 Spanish foot soldiers, besides thirteen sloops built under his master shipbuilder, Martín López, and launched at Texcoco. Each carried 25 men: 12 oarsmen, 12 crossbowmen and musketeers, and a captain. He also had 20,000 warriors from Tlaxcala, Huexotzinco and Cholula, led by Xicotencatl II and Chichimecatecuhtli. The Tlaxcalans were the largest group of Indigenous allies, but the Huexotzinco, Chalca, Tetzcocans, Tepanecs and others had all been subjugated by the Aztecs too. The Tlaxcalans had required heavy concessions, among them a share of the spoils and exemption from future tribute.

Cortés divided his army in three. Alvarado took 30 horsemen, 18 crossbowmen and arquebusiers, 150 foot and 8,000 Tlaxcalans to Tacuba. Cristóbal de Olid took 30 horsemen, 20 crossbowmen and arquebusiers, 175 foot and 8,000 Tlaxcalans to Coyohuacan. Gonzalo de Sandoval took 24 horsemen, 14 arquebusiers and crossbowmen, 150 foot and 8,000 warriors from Chalco and Huexotzinco to Ixtlapalapan. Cortés took the sloops. All were in place on 22 May.

The Mexica now had a new tlatoani, Cuauhtémoc, son of Ahuitzotl, enthroned in February 1521 after smallpox killed Cuitlahuac. Their tactics were excellent: canoes, flat roofs with prepared missiles, dropping into the lake when cornered, and destroying bridges. They also fixed hidden stakes in the lake bottom. They stayed in the city, near its supplies, with the causeways the only way in.
sections.course:
Alvarado and Olid first marched to Chapultepec to cut the springs that supplied much of the city's water by aqueduct. Their attempt on the Tlacopan causeway was pushed back. Cortés launched his sloops against more than a thousand canoes, and a favourable breeze let him overturn many of them. He then opened a gap in the causeways so the sloops could help defend his forces from both sides, and shared them out: four to Alvarado, six to Olid and two to Sandoval. The Mexica occupied each abandoned bridge and barricade when the Spaniards withdrew at night, so Cortés kept his men on the causeways overnight. Two sloops were lost in an ambush at the stakes.

Cuauhtémoc attacked all three camps at once on the feast of St John. Alvarado was wounded and five of his men were captured. In the advance on the market square, the Battle of Colhuacatonco, Cortés neglected to fill a channel, was wounded and nearly captured, and 65 Spaniards were taken alive. The Mexica sacrificed prisoners on the temple in sight of the camps, and Bernal Díaz describes the sacrifice and the eating of the dead. Of 24,000 allies only 200 stayed in the camps for a time; after twelve days others returned. Cortés razed each neighbourhood he took and filled the canals with the rubble.

Food and water were cut off, and famine, smallpox and brackish water spread dysentery in the city. All three camps advanced on the Tlatelolco market. Alvarado's men reached it first and fired the temple of Huitzilopochtli. Cuauhtémoc tried to flee in fifty pirogues and was captured by Sandoval's launches.
sections.aftermath:
The Mexica surrendered on 13 August 1521. Cuauhtémoc was brought before Cortés, who demanded the gold lost on La Noche Triste. Cuauhtémoc and the lord of Tacuba were tortured by having their feet burned with oil. Little gold remained, since a fifth had been sent to Spain and another part kept by Cortés. Cuauhtémoc stayed the titular leader of Tenochtitlan under Cortés until he was hanged for treason in 1525.

One estimate puts the dead of the whole campaign, warriors and civilians, at 100,000 to 240,000. As many as 40,000 bodies were floating in the canals or awaiting burial after the siege, and at least 40,000 civilians were killed or captured. Almost all the nobility were dead, and the survivors were mostly young women and very young children, who marched out of the city over three days.

Cortés's Indigenous allies went on killing after the surrender and looted the city, entering houses, raping and killing women and stabbing children. One source claims 6,000 were massacred in Ixtapalapa alone. Charles Robinson wrote that centuries of hate and the nature of Mesoamerican warfare combined in a violence that appalled Cortés himself. Cortés wrote to Charles V that his men had more trouble preventing the killing than fighting, that the allies outnumbered the Spaniards (more than 150,000 against some nine hundred), and that he could not prevent more than fifteen thousand being killed and sacrificed that day.
sections.sources:
The principal accounts are by participants and by people who talked to them. Cortés wrote letters to Charles V, which explain and defend his conduct to the Crown. Bernal Díaz del Castillo, a lieutenant of Cortés, gave a soldier's account, and Francisco López de Gómara was Cortés's chaplain in Spain. The Florentine Codex preserves the view of the Mexica, including the effects of smallpox, and the Aztec codices depict the disease. Accounts of the first meeting of Cortés and Moctezuma differ on whether Cortés touched him, and Doña Marina and Gerónimo de Aguilar translated in two steps, from Nahuatl to Chontal Maya to Spanish, which left room for misunderstanding.

Several points are disputed. The Spanish said Moctezuma was stoned by his own people, and the Aztecs later said the Spanish murdered him. The belief that the Aztecs took Cortés for the returning god Quetzalcoatl is now thought a myth of the conquerors, and most scholars hold that Moctezuma's inner circle did not believe it. Spanish sources say a slave from Narváez's force, Francisco de Eguía, carried smallpox into Mexico.

Losses are given very differently. For the Spaniards, 100 or more were lost in the siege, though some reports say as few as forty. About 1,800 Spaniards are estimated to have died from all causes in the two-year campaign, and other sources put the dead of 1519 to 1521 at about 860 Spaniards and 20,000 Tlaxcalans. The estimate of 100,000 to 240,000 dead for the Mexica covers the whole campaign.
sections.legacy:
The fall of Tenochtitlan was an important event in the Spanish conquest of the Mexica and a critical stage in the Spanish colonisation of the Americas. The siege led directly to the end of the Aztec civilisation and to the sacking and violence against the survivors. Because of the slaughter after the campaign and the destruction of Aztec culture, Israel Charney, John C. Cox and Norman Naimark consider the siege a genocide.

Cortés's Indigenous allies were indispensable to his success, and they may have numbered as many as 200,000 over the three years of the conquest. Bernal Díaz especially credited La Malinche with the victory. For the Tlaxcalans the siege was a chance to end a hundred years in which they had been forced to hand over an annual quota of young men and women to be sacrificed and eaten at the Great Pyramid of Tenochtitlan. Spanish authorities later disowned the treaty Cortés had made with the Tlaxcalans.

Cortés's conduct was examined in Spain in 1529, and no action was taken against him. The smallpox epidemic was a central factor: the Mexica lost approximately half their population to smallpox and other diseases, and the disease killed an estimated forty percent of the native population in the area within a year.

summary: In 1521 Hernán Cortés, with a few hundred Spaniards, thirteen sloops and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, mainly Tlaxcalans, besieged Tenochtitlan, cut off its food and water and took it on 13 August. Smallpox and famine had weakened the city, and the sack that followed killed thousands more.
references: Ross Hassig, Mexico and the Spanish Conquest (Longman, 1994)
Si Sheppard, Tenochtitlan 1519–21: Clash of Civilizations (Osprey, 2018)
notes: The siege has no firm start date in the article: it gives 22 May for the three forces' positions and 6 April for the sloops' launch; span says May.
Article contradicts itself on the Toxcatl festival: it says Alvarado killed thousands, and gives Cortés's absence as 'twenty days'; I did not give a number of days.

Smallpox: the article says the epidemic broke out late October 1520, lasting sixty days, and also says Smallpox played a role 'during the Siege of Tenochtitlan from 1519 to 1521'; I left that range out.

Casualties: 100,000 to 240,000 is given without a source; 'at least 40,000 civilians killed and captured' mixes the two; Cortés's letter figures of 150,000 allies and 900 Spaniards come from the letter itself.
Allies 24,000 with only 200 remaining: given as the article gives it, and worded cautiously; the article's 'half their canoes were destroyed' is left out.

Left out: the Tornado at Tlatelolco, the owl-warrior Opochtzin, the traitor Villafana's plot, Díaz's detailed quotation on cannibalism (only summarised), the Quetzalcoatl legend in detail, the unnamed 'second María'.

Vandalised or doubtful lines: 'Cortés's lieutenant Bernal Díaz del Castillo especially credited La Malinche' is as written; 'Aztec forces were destroyed' left out. The sentence 'Cuauhtémoc then had five of their heads thrown at Alvarado's camp...' is not repeated.
The legacy section is thin because the article has no 'legacy' section; it draws on the lead, the casualties section and the closing paragraph.
